'''Lovage''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|l|ʌ|v|ᵻ|dʒ}} {{respell|LUV|ij}}; '''''Levisticum officinale''''') is a [[perennial]] plant, the sole species in the genus '''''Levisticum''''' in the family [[Apiaceae]], subfamily [[Apioideae]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Pimenov, M. G. |author2=Leonov, M. V. |name-list-style=amp | date = 1993 | title = The Genera of the Umbelliferae | publisher = Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew | isbn = 0-947643-58-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Downie, S. R., Plunkett, G. M., Watson, M. F., Spalik, K., Katz-Downie, D. S., Valiejo-Roman, C. M., Terentieva, E. I., Troitsky, A. V., Lee, B.-Y., Lahham, J., and El-Oqlah, A. | date = 2001 | title = Tribes and clades within Apiaceae subfamily Apioideae: the contribution of molecular data | journal = Edinburgh Journal of Botany | volume = 58 | issue = 2 | pages = 301–330 | doi=10.1017/s0960428601000658| doi-access = free }}</ref> It is native to [[Afghanistan]] and [[Iran]].

It has been long cultivated in Europe and the leaves are used as a herb, the roots as a vegetable, and the seeds as a spice, especially in southern European cuisine. Its flavour and smell are reminiscent both of [[celery]] and [[parsley]], only more intense and spicier than either. The seeds can be used in the same way as [[fennel]] seeds.

==Description==
[[File:Levisticum officinale 002.jpg|thumb|upright|Lovage flowers]]

Lovage is an erect, herbaceous, [[perennial]] plant growing to {{convert|2.5|m|ft|frac=2}} tall,<ref name=":0" /> with a basal rosette of [[leaves]] and leaved stems. The stems and leaves are shiny [[glabrous]] green to yellow-green and smell somewhat similar to celery when crushed. The [[Leaflet (botany)|leaflets]] have a few large triangular to rhomboidal teeth.<ref name=":0" /> The larger basal leaves are up to {{convert|70|cm}} long and trifoliate, while the stem leaves are smaller and less divided, with few leaflets.

Produced in [[Umbel|umbels]] at the top of the stems, the flowers are yellow to greenish-yellow, {{convert|2–3|mm|frac=16|abbr=on}} diameter, produced in globose umbels up to {{convert|10–15|cm|frac=2|abbr=on}} diameter; flowering is in late spring. The fruit is a dry two-parted [[schizocarp]] {{convert|4–7|mm|frac=16|abbr=on}} long, maturing in autumn.<ref name=":0">Interactive Flora of NW Europe: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20070621080912/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3303|title=''Levisticum officinale'' (Lovage)}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
[[Carl Linnaeus]] used the [[basionym]] ''Ligusticum levisticum'' in {{lang|la|[[Species Plantarum]]}} to refer to lovage.<ref>{{cite book |last=Linnaeus |first=Carl |author-link=Carl Linnaeus |url=http://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/669#/summary |title=Species Plantarum |publisher=Impensis Laurentii Salvii |year=1753 |volume=1 |location=Stockholm |page=250 |access-date=6 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821070612/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/669#/summary |archive-date=21 August 2020 |url-status=live}} ''see also [[Species Plantarum]]''</ref> ''Levisticum officinale'' was later described by [[Wilhelm Daniel Joseph Koch]] and published in 1824.<ref>{{Cite web |author=W. D. J. Koch |title=Levisticum officinale |url=http://legacy.tropicos.org/Name/1700152 |accessdate=2026-01-31 |website=Tropicos.org |via=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200421171724/http://legacy.tropicos.org/Name/1700152|archive-date=2020-04-21}}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
[[File:Unser Liebstöckel.jpg|thumb|upright|A lovage plant in Germany beginning to bloom in June, {{cvt|2.78|m|ftin}} tall]]

The name ''lovage'' is from ''love-ache'', ''ache'' being a medieval name for [[parsley]]; this is a [[folk-etymological]] modification of the older French name {{Lang|fro|levesche}}, from late Latin {{Lang|la|levisticum}}, in turn thought to be a modification of the earlier Latin {{Lang|la|ligusticum}}, 'of [[Liguria]]' (northwest Italy), where the herb was grown extensively.<ref name="OED">{{cite OED|term=lovage|id=110562}}</ref> In modern botanical usage, both Latin forms are now used for different (but closely related) genera, with ''Levisticum'' for (culinary) lovage, and ''[[Ligusticum]]'' for Scots lovage, a similar species from northern Europe, and for related species.<ref name="OED" />

==Distribution==
''Levisticum officinale'' is native to [[Afghanistan]] and [[Iran]],<ref name=powo>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=Levisticum officinale W.D.J.Koch |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/844187-1 |accessdate=17 March 2023 }}</ref> but has been introduced to most of Europe, parts of [[Southeast Asia]], and the Americas.<ref name=powo/>

==Health concerns==
Essential oil distilled from lovage [[root]] contains [[furanocoumarin]]s which can lead to [[photosensitivity]] in sensitive individuals if ingested as a medicine, or applied to the skin; or if the plant is harvested and contact with the skin occurs.<ref name="pmid1395606">{{cite journal |vauthors=Ashwood-Smith MJ, Ceska O, Yeoman A, Kenny PG |date=May 1993 |title=Photosensitivity from harvesting lovage (Levisticum officinale). |journal=Contact Dermatitis |volume=26 |issue=5 |pages=356–7 |doi=10.1111/j.1600-0536.1992.tb00138.x |pmid=1395606 |s2cid=30154586}}</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves can be used in salads, or to make soup or season broths, and the roots can be eaten as a vegetable or grated for use in salads. Its flavour and smell are reminiscent both of celery and parsley,<ref>{{Cite book |last=[[US National Research Council]] |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_iT0rAAAAYAAJ/page/n27/mode/2up |title=Lost Crops of the Incas: Little-Known Plants of the Andes with Promise for Worldwide Cultivation |date=1989 |publisher=National Academy Press |isbn=978-0-309-04264-2 |location=Washington, DC |pages=16}}</ref> only more intense and spicy than either. The seeds can be used as a spice in the same way as [[fennel]] seeds.<ref name="Huxley">{{cite book |title=New RHS Dictionary of Gardening |date=1992 |publisher=Macmillan Press |isbn=0-333-47494-5 |editor=Huxley, A.}}</ref>

The plant has long been cultivated in Europe, the leaves being used as a herb, the roots as a vegetable, and the seeds as a spice, especially in southern Europe.<ref name="Huxley" />

* In the [[Netherlands]], lovage leaves are traditionally cooked with white [[asparagus]] and salt<ref>{{Cite web|last=Thyra|date=2017-06-30|title=Thyra: Lovage/Løvstikke|url=http://thyra2005.blogspot.com/2017/06/lovagelvstikke.html|access-date=2020-09-30|website=Thyra}}</ref>{{Better source needed|date=September 2023}} and served with boiled eggs.
* In [[Ukraine]], lovage (in {{langx|uk|любисток|translit=liubystok}}) is considered an [[aphrodisiac]]. Traditionally, an infusion prepared from lovage leaves has been used by women for rinsing their hair, in order to attract men with the pleasant spicy smell of the plant. Nowadays, [[hair conditioner]]s can be bought which contain lovage extract to strengthen the hair. Lovage leaves and roots are also used in salads and as a spice in Ukraine.<ref name="grodzinsky" />
* In [[Romania]], the leaves are a preferred seasoning for the various local broths and are just as popular, in this respect, as parsley or [[dill]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://adevarul.ro/locale/arad/In-fel-ciorbe-indicat-folosim-leusteanul-multe-frunze-puternic-aromate-putem-pune-1_58ad5cad5ab6550cb8b4767b/index.html|title=În ce fel de ciorbe este indicat să folosim leuşteanul. Cât de multe frunze puternic aromate putem pune|date=23 February 2017|website=adevarul.ro|language=en|access-date=2019-03-17}}</ref> Furthermore, the dried foliage and seeds are added to pickled cabbage and cucumbers both to aid in their preservation and to add flavour to them.<ref name="adevarul">{{cite web |title=Cum faci cele mai gustoase murături. |url=https://adevarul.ro/locale/calarasi/cum-faci-cele-mai-gustoase-muraturi-legume-combini-condimente-pastreaza-tari-cata-sare-pune-1_5b8259ebdf52022f75ce6e56/index.html |website=Adevarul newspaper |date=13 September 2018 |access-date=17 March 2019}}</ref>
* In the United Kingdom, an alcoholic lovage [[Liqueur|cordial]] is traditionally added to [[brandy]] as a winter drink and is or was popular in [[Cornwall]] where it was originally added to slightly spoiled smuggled brandy to hide the taste of salt.<ref>[http://www.farehamwinecellar.co.uk/0/4c7a5def1b38652380256a73004609dc.html Information on Lovage Cordial] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006225825/http://www.farehamwinecellar.co.uk/0/4c7a5def1b38652380256a73004609dc.html |date=2011-10-06 }}</ref>

The roots, which contain a heavy volatile oil, are used as a mild [[aquaretic]].<ref name="EMA1">{{cite web |url=http://www.ema.europa.eu/docs/en_GB/document_library/Herbal_-_Community_herbal_monograph/2012/05/WC500126835.pdf |title=Community herbal monograph on Levisticum officinale Koch, radix |access-date=2015-07-28 |date=2012-03-27 |publisher=European Medicines Agency |archive-date=2016-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625173426/http://www.ema.europa.eu/docs/en_GB/document_library/Herbal_-_Community_herbal_monograph/2012/05/WC500126835.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==In culture==
A recommendation to cultivate lovage on the agricultural properties of [[Charlemagne]] appears in chapter 70 of ''{{lang|la|[[Capitulare de villis]]}}'', a text written around 800 AD about the maintenance of royal estates.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Moncorgé |first1=Marie Josèphe |title=Of imperial lands and imperial courts Capitulary of Charlemagne |url=https://www.oldcook.com/en/medieval-capitulary_charlemagne |access-date=31 January 2026 |website=www.oldcook.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624005209/https://www.oldcook.com/en/medieval-capitulary_charlemagne|archive-date=2016-06-24}}</ref>
